subject: Chemistry
title: Stoichiometry & Gas Laws
outline: The mole, Avogadro's constant and molar mass
Stoichiometry, limiting reagent and percentage yield
Boyle's, Charles's and the pressure law
General gas equation and the ideal gas equation PV = nRT

modules.title: 4.1 The Mole Concept
modules.html:
The mole is the amount of substance that contains as many elementary entities as there are atoms in 12 g of carbon-12. That number is the Avogadro constant, \( N_A = 6.02\times10^{23}\ \mathrm{mol^{-1}} \).

One mole of any substance contains \(6.02\times10^{23}\) particles and has a mass in grams equal to its relative atomic or molecular mass (the molar mass, g mol⁻¹).

\( n = \dfrac{m}{M} = \dfrac{N}{N_A} = \dfrac{V_{\text{gas at s.t.p.}}}{22.4\ \mathrm{dm^3}} = C \times \dfrac{V_{\text{soln}}}{1000} \)

  • Mass ↔ mole: 40 g of NaOH (M = 40) is 1 mol.
  • Particles: 0.5 mol of CO2 contains \(0.5\times6.02\times10^{23}=3.01\times10^{23}\) molecules, but three times that many atoms.
  • Gas volume: at s.t.p. (0 °C, 760 mmHg) one mole of any gas occupies 22.4 dm³; at r.t.p. (25 °C, 1 atm) about 24 dm³. This is the molar volume.
  • Solutions: a 0.1 mol dm⁻³ solution contains 0.1 mol in every 1000 cm³.

Molar mass calculations

M(CaCO3) = 40 + 12 + (3×16) = 100 g mol⁻¹. M(CuSO4·5H2O) = 64 + 32 + 64 + 5(18) = 250 g mol⁻¹.

Percentage composition

\( \%\text{element} = \dfrac{\text{total mass of the element in 1 mole}}{\text{molar mass}} \times 100 \)

In CaCO3: %Ca = 40/100 × 100 = 40%; %C = 12%; %O = 48%.

examples.q: Calculate the number of moles in 9.8 g of H2SO4 (M = 98).
What volume does 3.2 g of oxygen occupy at s.t.p.? (O = 16)
How many atoms are present in 0.25 mol of water?

modules.title: 4.2 Empirical and Molecular Formulae
modules.html:
The empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms in a compound; the molecular formula gives the actual number of atoms in one molecule and is always a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula.

\( \text{Molecular formula} = (\text{empirical formula})_n,\qquad n=\dfrac{\text{molar mass}}{\text{empirical formula mass}} \)

Standard working method

  1. Write the mass (or percentage) of each element.
  2. Divide each by the relative atomic mass to get moles.
  3. Divide all the answers by the smallest of them.
  4. Multiply if necessary to clear fractions (×2 for .5, ×3 for .33).

Worked example. A compound contains 40% C, 6.7% H and 53.3% O; its molar mass is 180.

Element%÷ Ar÷ smallest
C4040/12 = 3.331
H6.76.7/1 = 6.72
O53.353.3/16 = 3.331

Empirical formula CH2O (mass 30); n = 180/30 = 6; molecular formula C6H12O6 — glucose.

Stoichiometry from equations

Coefficients in a balanced equation give the mole ratio. For \( \mathrm{2H_2 + O_2 \rightarrow 2H_2O} \), 2 mol of hydrogen need 1 mol of oxygen and yield 2 mol of water. The reactant that finishes first is the limiting reagent; it fixes the yield.

\( \%\text{yield} = \dfrac{\text{actual yield}}{\text{theoretical yield}}\times100 \)

Volumetric analysis

For a titration \( \dfrac{C_AV_A}{C_BV_B} = \dfrac{n_A}{n_B} \), where nA and nB are the stoichiometric coefficients of acid and base.

examples.q: 25.0 cm³ of 0.1 M NaOH is exactly neutralised by 20.0 cm³ of HCl. Find the concentration of the acid.
A hydrocarbon contains 85.7% C and 14.3% H, molar mass 56. Find its molecular formula.
examples.a: C: 85.7/12 = 7.14; H: 14.3/1 = 14.3; ratio 1:2 so empirical CH2 (14). n = 56/14 = 4, molecular formula C4H8.

modules.title: 4.3 The Gas Laws
modules.html:
Boyle's law

At constant temperature, the volume of a fixed mass of gas is inversely proportional to its pressure: \( V \propto \frac{1}{P} \), so \( P_1V_1 = P_2V_2 \). A graph of V against 1/P is a straight line through the origin.

Charles's law

At constant pressure, volume is directly proportional to absolute temperature: \( \frac{V_1}{T_1}=\frac{V_2}{T_2} \), where T is in kelvin (K = °C + 273).

Pressure (Gay-Lussac's) law

At constant volume, \( \frac{P_1}{T_1}=\frac{P_2}{T_2} \).

General gas equation

\( \dfrac{P_1V_1}{T_1}=\dfrac{P_2V_2}{T_2} \qquad\text{and}\qquad PV = nRT \)

where R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ (or 0.0821 atm dm³ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹). This ideal gas equation combines all the gas laws.

Dalton's law of partial pressures

The total pressure of a mixture of non-reacting gases is the sum of the partial pressures: \( P_T = P_1+P_2+\dots \). When a gas is collected over water, \( P_{\text{dry gas}} = P_{\text{total}} - P_{\text{water vapour}} \).

Graham's law of diffusion

\( \dfrac{R_1}{R_2}=\sqrt{\dfrac{M_2}{M_1}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{\rho_2}{\rho_1}} \)

The rate of diffusion of a gas is inversely proportional to the square root of its density (or molar mass) at constant temperature and pressure. Hydrogen diffuses four times faster than oxygen because \(\sqrt{32/2}=4\).

Gay-Lussac's law of combining volumes and Avogadro's law

When gases react, the volumes of reactants and products, measured at the same temperature and pressure, are in simple whole-number ratios. Avogadro's law adds that equal volumes of all gases under the same conditions contain equal numbers of molecules. Hence for \( \mathrm{N_2 + 3H_2 \rightarrow 2NH_3} \), 1 volume of nitrogen and 3 volumes of hydrogen give 2 volumes of ammonia.

Ideal versus real gases

An ideal gas obeys the gas laws exactly; its molecules have negligible volume and no intermolecular attractions. Real gases deviate at high pressure and low temperature, where molecules are close enough for attractions and their own volume to matter — that is why gases can be liquefied.

examples.q: A gas occupies 250 cm³ at 27 °C and 760 mmHg. What is its volume at s.t.p.?
Compare the rates of diffusion of SO2 (M = 64) and CH4 (M = 16).
examples.a: R(CH4)/R(SO2) = √(64/16) = 2, so methane diffuses twice as fast.

examples.q: Why do real gases deviate from ideal behaviour at low temperature?
examples.a: At low temperature molecules move slowly, so intermolecular attractive forces (neglected in the ideal model) become significant and the actual volume is smaller than predicted.
